scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The origins of Poomaruthan Theyyam are rooted in the migration myths of the Thiyya community in North Malabar.
The deity is described as a guard of Shiva origin who resided within a blossoming flower in the form of wind.
He became a 'brotherly friend' to the goddess Poomala Devi after helping her in a heavenly garden.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Poomaruthan Theyyam is performed during the annual festivals of Poomala shrines.
It represents the protection of the goddess and the community.
The act of the deity hitting onlookers with a shield is a significant ritual event, believed to be a form of divine engagement.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by 'lively movements' that emphasize martial skill.
The performer holds a sword and a wooden shield, which are the primary tools of the choreography.
The movement involves 'twirling the shield and swinging the sword' in rhythmic patterns.
Watch for Shield Knock, Shield Twirl.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: While the specific percussion patterns are not detailed in the sources, the performance is described as 'ritualistic dance' accompanied by 'lively movements.' In the context of North Malabar Theyyam, this typically involves the Chenda (drum) and Elathalam (cymbals) to provide the rhythmic structure for the sword and shield play.
The shouting of the valyakars serves as a vocal accompaniment that drives the energy of the performance.
Listen for the Chenda (implied by tradition), Elathalam (implied by tradition).
The soundscape is dominated by the rhythmic clashing of the wooden shield and sword, punctuated by the high-energy shouts of the valyakars who gather to provoke and excite the deity.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The deity Poomaruthan is the central figure, described as a 'Hindu god' of Shiva origin.
The Arya princess Aryapoonkani is also central to the myth, as she was possessed by Poomala and traveled with Poomaruthan on the wooden ship.
Variants are linked to specific temple myths.

Poomaruthan is classified as a 'Theyyam' and an 'Indian folk dance.' It belongs to the broader tradition of North Malabar Theyyam, specifically associated with the 'Shiva origin' deities and the 'Thiyya community' worship practices.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Poomaruthan Theyyam is a sacred ritual where the performer is believed to be the living embodiment of the deity. Respectful distance should be maintained unless the deity initiates contact. Photography may be restricted in certain inner sanctums of the Poomala shrines.

wardrobe.from_sources: The costume features 'special face art and body art' created from natural substances. A defining feature is the 'black mustache and beard' worn on the face. The performer wears a 'Mudi,' a large wooden crown-like ornamentation. The size of the Mudi changes according to the time of the ritual: a 'small Mudi' is used for the night Vellattam, while a 'large Mudi' is used for the daytime Theyyam. The setting is typically the 'shrine of the regional Hindu goddess Poomala bhagavathy' or associated temple grounds in Kannur and Kasaragod.
